accounts.status: Not consulted. Named as a catalogue of the Old Babylonian plaques. The house, its paint, the potter and the man from the palace are invented.

citation: British Museum. The Queen of the Night (the Burney Relief), museum number 2003,0718.1. Collection online record.

accounts.status: Read on 17 October 2026 in search-returned page text from the record, and in the same description reproduced on a MyMiniFactory page: baked straw-tempered clay, painted red, black and white; superimposed horns; lowered wings; a black ground; purchase as the principal acquisition for the Museum’s 250th anniversary in 2003; the renaming on the basis of a limerick by Frances Carey, then Head of National Programmes; the title’s earlier use for a character in Mozart’s Magic Flute, a song and a night-blooming cactus. The limerick is not quoted.
accounts.use: The figure and its paint (II); the name taken from a limerick and already held (VI).

citation: The Queen under attack: a rejoinder. Iraq (British Institute for the Study of Iraq), 2007.

accounts.status: Opening paragraphs read on 17 October 2026 in search-returned page text from Cambridge Core: a mould-made plaque of straw-tempered clay; the horned headdress, lowered wings, dewclaws and talons, the rod-and-ring in each hand, the addorsed lions and the owls; traces of black, red and white paint; Pauline Albenda’s 1970 conclusion that the relief is not genuine; the author’s conviction that it is a genuine work of the age of Hammurabi. The author is not named in the text read; it is attributed to Dominique Collon here, whose earlier work on the plaque it cites, unchecked. Volume and pages not checked. The rest of the article was not read.
accounts.use: The large one, its making and its age (II); the scholar who called it modern and the curator who answered her (VI).

citation: Burney Relief. Wikipedia.

accounts.status: Read on 17 October 2026 in search-returned page text: a Syrian dealer who may have acquired the plaque in southern Iraq in 1924; the Museum’s refusal to buy it in 1935; Sidney Burney; Norman Colville; after Colville’s death, the purchase at auction by Goro Sakamoto and the refused export licence; the loan to the Museum from 1980 to 1991; the purchase in 2003 for £1,500,000. accounts.use: The find-spot nobody wrote down, the dealers, the collector, the buyer from Japan, the eleven-year loan and the purchase (VI); the burnishing and the fine lines cut by hand (II).

accounts.status: Read on 17 October 2026 in search-returned page text. It quotes Dominique Collon on the making (stiff clay folded and pushed into a shaped mould, more clay pressed in behind) and on the caption of the first published photograph, in the Illustrated London News of 1936: Ishtar, whose supporting owls present a problem. The caption is known here only through that quotation.
accounts.use: How the large one was made (II); the newspaper that called her Ishtar and found the owls a problem (III).
